h: Hidden skulls and a horse with attitude
p: Every big gallery has its party tricks, and the National Gallery has some of the best. Hans Holbein's The Ambassadors shows two smartly dressed men surrounded by globes, books and instruments, but there's a strange smear across the floor in front of them. Walk to the right-hand side of the painting, look back along it at a low angle, and the smear snaps into a skull. Kids love it, and so do most grown-ups.

A few more to hunt out: Leonardo da Vinci's The Virgin of the Rocks, glowing in its dim, rocky setting; Velázquez's Rokeby Venus; Seurat's sunny Bathers at Asnières; and George Stubbs's Whistlejacket, a life-size rearing racehorse with no background at all, which is a lot more dramatic in person than it sounds. Monet's water lilies are always a crowd-pleaser on a grey afternoon too.

The gallery marked its 200th birthday in 2024, and the Sainsbury Wing, home to many of the earliest paintings, was given a fresh new entrance as part of the celebrations. Use the free floor plan to pick a route, and remember you don't have to see everything. An hour with a handful of favourites can be far more satisfying than a three-hour trudge.

Outside, Trafalgar Square has its own entertainment. Nelson's Column and the lions are obvious photo stops, and the Fourth Plinth hosts a changing contemporary artwork that always gets people talking. Across the road, St Martin-in-the-Fields is known for its concerts and has a café down in the crypt that makes a cosy spot for a warming bowl of soup.
